nodes.label: Execution Model
nodes.rationale: Contracts run as Wasm guests in a sandboxed host inside stellar-core. A transaction is the atomicity boundary: errors, panics, missing auth, and budget exhaustion roll back every ledger change, including nested writes. A caller can catch a callee error with try_ client methods and continue. Guest code holds host objects by integer handles, and the host meters every step.

nodes.label: Env
nodes.rationale: Everything a contract can reach hangs off Env: storage, events, crypto, ledger, deployer, prng, current_contract_address, and invoke_contract. The only clock is env.ledger().timestamp().

nodes.label: env.prng
nodes.rationale: env.prng() is seeded from ledger state and is predictable. Never use it for keys, authorization, or high-stakes randomness.

nodes.label: Reentrancy
nodes.rationale: The host blocks direct and indirect reentrancy on normal calls. External calls are still failure, budget, and side-effect boundaries, so state updates must be ordered deliberately.

nodes.label: Storage
nodes.rationale: Instance, persistent, and temporary storage have different lifetimes and costs. Choosing the wrong type is a top source of bugs and fee waste. Contract state lives in storage, never in the #[contract] struct.

nodes.label: Instance Storage
nodes.rationale: Instance storage shares one TTL with the contract instance, so one extend_ttl warms every global. It is capped at the network max entry size (64KB serialized on mainnet). Never put per-user or unbounded data there. Use it for an admin address, config, and other small global state.

nodes.label: Persistent Storage
nodes.rationale: Persistent entries have a per-key TTL. When they expire they are archived, not deleted, and can be restored. Use them for user balances and anything that must survive being untouched.

nodes.label: Temporary Storage
nodes.rationale: Temporary entries have a per-key TTL and are deleted permanently when they expire. They are the cheapest fit for caches, time-bounded data, and oracle prices. There is no restore path.

nodes.label: TTL
nodes.rationale: TTL is counted in ledgers, about 5 seconds each and 17280 per day. On mainnet, new persistent entries start near 120 days, temporary entries near 1 day, and no entry can exceed about 180 days. Since protocol 23, archived persistent entries in the read-write footprint are restored automatically and rent is paid again. Temporary expiry means deleted. TTL expiry is not a security mechanism: if data must become invalid after a deadline, store the deadline in the value and check it. Code should not assume a previously written entry is still present.

nodes.label: extend_ttl
nodes.rationale: extend_ttl(threshold, extend_to) is a no-op unless the current TTL is below the threshold, then it sets TTL to extend_to. It is idempotent and never shortens. Extending on every write, so active users pay for their own state, is the standard per-user pattern. Extending instance TTL at busy entry points keeps globals alive. Rent is charged at invocation time.

nodes.label: extend_ttl_with_limits
nodes.rationale: Protocol 26 added extend_ttl_with_limits for persistent and instance storage so callers cannot force arbitrary rent costs. It takes extend_to, min_extension, and max_extension.

nodes.label: ExtendFootprintTTLOp
nodes.rationale: Anyone can extend any entry's TTL with ExtendFootprintTTLOp and no contract authorization. Benevolent keep-alive services are possible, which is why expiry cannot enforce a permission deadline.

nodes.label: Typed Storage Keys
nodes.rationale: A #[contracttype] key enum centralizes the schema and prevents collisions. Adding variants is the forward-compatible way to grow storage. Fine-grained keys let unrelated transactions run in parallel; one giant Map serializes callers and makes every caller pay to read all of it.

nodes.label: Read-Write Footprint
nodes.rationale: Every transaction declares its read/write footprint up front. Transactions that touch the same read-write entry serialize. Everything touched must be in the footprint whether or not it is used, and each entry has a fixed cost plus bytes.

nodes.label: i128
nodes.rationale: i128 is the canonical SEP-41 token amount and admits negatives, so inputs must reject amount < 0.

nodes.label: U256 and I256
nodes.rationale: U256 and I256 are the 256-bit types. Their checked arithmetic methods return Option and require protocol 26 or later.

nodes.label: MuxedAddress
nodes.rationale: MuxedAddress distinguishes sub-accounts of one address for exchanges and custodians. Token transfer accepts it as the destination, and a plain Address converts into it.

nodes.label: Address
nodes.rationale: There is no msg.sender. Pass the acting Address explicitly and require_auth it. require_auth on a user-supplied who proves control of who, not that who is allowed to act. Privileged paths must load the admin from storage and authorize that address.

nodes.label: Authorization
nodes.rationale: Authorization is host-mediated and explicit. Require it when a call spends, reduces, reconfigures, or consumes an address's authority downstream. Reading public data and crediting a balance need no auth.

nodes.label: require_auth
nodes.rationale: require_auth asks whether that address authorized this contract, this function, and these exact arguments in this transaction. The host supplies replay protection with nonces and expiration, so contracts do not track nonces. Stellar accounts satisfy auth at their medium threshold.

nodes.label: require_auth_for_args
nodes.rationale: require_auth_for_args narrows the signed payload to the arguments you pass. That supports partial commitments, such as signing a max amount while the contract enforces actual <= max.

nodes.label: Auth Trees
nodes.rationale: A user signs a tree of invocations, not a single call. require_auth deeper in the stack passes only if the path and arguments match the signed tree, and each tree node matches at most once. Auth does not cascade, so authorizing A.foo does not let every contract A calls claim that auth. Refactoring the call graph changes the tree and silently breaks signers of the old shape. SDKs build the tree from simulation. The most common real-world bug is failing to re-auth at every layer that uses an address's authority.

nodes.label: authorize_as_current_contract
nodes.rationale: When contract A directly calls B, B may require_auth A's address; the direct call authorizes only that immediate invocation. If B will make a deeper call that needs A's auth, A must pre-authorize it with authorize_as_current_contract.

nodes.label: Custom Accounts
nodes.rationale: A contract address can act as an account, such as a smart wallet, multisig, or passkey wallet, by implementing CustomAccountInterface. Keep the check lean because its cost is added to every transaction the account signs.

nodes.label: __check_auth
nodes.rationale: The host calls __check_auth with a host-computed signature_payload digest, the signature artifact, and auth_contexts for the calls this auth would cover. Always verify signature_payload itself; verifying any other message authorizes arbitrary calls. Use auth_contexts for spend limits and function allowlists. Never require_auth the account's own address inside __check_auth, because that function is evaluating auth rather than consuming it.

nodes.label: CAP-71 Auth Delegation
nodes.rationale: Protocol 27 (CAP-71) lets a modular account delegate authentication inside __check_auth. get_delegated_signers returns unsanitized addresses supplied by the transaction, so the account must check that they are registered delegates before delegate_auth forwards the current check. Delegation can nest and does not need a separate auth entry per delegate.

nodes.label: __constructor
nodes.rationale: Prefer __constructor over a separate initialize function because it removes the front-running window between deploy and init. The name must be exact, it runs only at creation, failure aborts deployment atomically, and a contract deployed without a constructor cannot gain one later.

nodes.label: Cross-contract Calls
nodes.rationale: Callee errors abort the caller unless the call uses try_ client methods. There is no msg.sender: pass the acting Address and require_auth it.

nodes.label: contractimport
nodes.rationale: contractimport! of another contract's WASM generates a typed client when the interface is known at compile time.

nodes.label: TokenClient
nodes.rationale: The SDK ships TokenClient for anything that implements the standard token interface, including every Stellar asset through its SAC, so no WASM import is required.

nodes.label: invoke_contract
nodes.rationale: env.invoke_contract is the untyped dynamic call for an interface that is not known at compile time.

nodes.label: Contract Events
nodes.rationale: Emit an event for every state change you want to index or audit. Events are much cheaper than storing queryable state, but they are ephemeral: RPC providers typically retain about 7 days, so long-term data must be derivable from on-chain state. Diagnostic log! events are off by default and are not part of consensus, so logic must not depend on them. Topics are how indexers filter.

nodes.label: contractevent
nodes.rationale: #[contractevent] replaces the deprecated env.events().publish. The snake-cased name is the first topic unless topics are overridden. data_format may be map, vec, or single-value; SEP-41 token events use single-value for a lone data field.

nodes.label: contracterror
nodes.rationale: Returning Result gives callers typed errors. Generated clients expose foo(), which panics on error, and try_foo(), where the inner Err is the contract error and the outer Err is a host failure such as budget, bad auth, or a type mismatch. Use panic_with_error! rather than a bare panic, which surfaces as an opaque host error. Error codes are public ABI and must never be renumbered across upgrades. An Err or panic rolls back all state changes of the invocation, including nested writes.

nodes.label: SEP-41
nodes.rationale: SEP-41 is the token interface. transfer, approve, and burn authorize from; transfer_from and burn_from authorize the spender, because the allowance already authorized from. Reads need no auth. mint, clawback, set_admin, set_authorized, and trust are SAC admin surface, not SEP-41. Wallets and indexers depend on the standard transfer, approve, mint, burn, and clawback event shapes.

nodes.label: Stellar Asset Contract
nodes.rationale: Every classic Stellar asset, including native XLM, exposes SEP-41 through its SAC. G-account balances live in trustlines with a 64-bit cap, and a missing or unauthorized trustline fails the transfer. C-account balances live in contract storage at full i128. Issuer flags apply, including AUTH_REQUIRED, AUTH_REVOCABLE freezes, and clawback. Transfers to the issuer burn and transfers from the issuer mint. A protocol that accepts arbitrary token addresses must survive all of this. The SAC adds the SEP-0011 asset string as a trailing event topic.

nodes.label: StellarAssetClient
nodes.rationale: StellarAssetClient is the SAC admin surface: mint, clawback, set_admin, set_authorized, and trust (protocol 26+). It is not the SEP-41 client.

nodes.label: Token Allowances
nodes.rationale: approve(from, spender, amount, expiration_ledger) expires. The convention is temporary storage keyed by (from, spender) with a TTL matching the expiration. Re-approving overwrites, so a spender can front-run a reduction and spend the old amount plus the new one. Mitigate by approving to 0 first or by using exact-amount auth instead of a standing allowance.

nodes.label: Upgradeability
nodes.rationale: Decide early whether the contract is mutable. Gate upgrade behind admin or governance auth. Upload the new WASM first and pass its hash to update_current_contract_wasm. The address and all storage survive; only the executable changes, and __constructor does not re-run. Storage schema is the contract's problem: reading an old key with a changed contracttype shape fails to decode. Store a schema version, add enum variants rather than reshaping them, and ship an idempotent admin-gated migrate that requires new_version > current_version.

nodes.label: SEP-0049
nodes.rationale: SEP-0049 standardizes upgradeable-contract interfaces.

nodes.label: OpenZeppelin stellar-contracts
nodes.rationale: OpenZeppelin stellar-contracts ships audited implementations of the upgradeable-contract interfaces.

nodes.label: Factories
nodes.rationale: Factory addresses are deterministic per deployer and salt. deployed_address computes one without deploying. Authorize who may deploy, emit an event per deployment so instances are indexable, and keep factory logic separate from instance business logic.

nodes.label: Deployer
nodes.rationale: env.deployer() updates the current contract WASM and deploys new instances. with_address(current contract, salt) plus deploy_v2(wasm_hash, constructor_args) is the factory path.

nodes.label: Governance Timelock
nodes.rationale: For upgrades and config changes, prefer a timelock: propose stores the action and an execute-after ledger, execute enforces the delay, and cancel lets governance abort. For multisig, separate proposer, approver, and executor, store proposals in persistent storage, and prevent replay with unique IDs, expiry, and explicit events. A custom account is often cleaner than in-contract multisig.

nodes.label: DeFi Patterns
nodes.rationale: Vaults should track total assets and shares, round conservatively on mint and redeem, and include pause controls. AMMs must define the invariant and fee accounting and slippage-check every user-facing swap. Oracles need freshness bounds, multi-source or median feeds, and circuit breakers. Regulated tokens should isolate allowlist, denylist, freeze, and forced-transfer logic in dedicated entrypoints with strong auth, emit policy-decision events, and never store PII on-chain.

nodes.label: Fees and Resource Limits
nodes.rationale: Contract transactions pay an inclusion fee plus a resource fee for CPU instructions, ledger reads and writes, transaction size, events size, and rent. Rent and events are refundable if unused; instructions and I/O are charged as declared, so submitters simulate first. If state diverges from simulation, costs can shift, so leave headroom. Quoted mainnet ceilings, including 400M CPU, 40MB memory, 200 reads and writes, 128KB WASM, and 64KB ledger entries, change by validator vote. Minimize distinct ledger entries, cap unbounded loops, and treat crypto verification inside __check_auth as the expensive primitive.

nodes.label: Contract Size
nodes.rationale: The 128KB WASM limit is real. The release profile in the skill setup is mandatory, and stellar contract build optimizes by default. If the binary is still too large, drop heavy dependencies such as full serde and regex, split the contract, or avoid large static data.
